section.title: Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
section.sectionRationale: Grieved by John's death, Jesus withdraws, yet has compassion on the crowds and feeds five thousand from five loaves and two fish, the only miracle in all four Gospels. That same night He walks to His disciples on the storm-tossed sea, rescues sinking Peter, and stills the wind, drawing from the boat the first full confession: truly You are the Son of God.
section.thesis: The compassionate Shepherd who feeds the multitude in the wilderness from almost nothing is the divine Lord who walks upon the sea and speaks the name of God, so that His provision and His mastery over creation together compel the worship of His disciples: truly You are the Son of God.
section.frameNote: Three beats: compassion and the feeding of the five thousand; Jesus walking on the water and rescuing Peter, leading to worship; and the healings at Gennesaret.

units.label: Compassion and the feeding
units.note: five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets

verses.text: When Jesus heard about John, He withdrew by boat privately to a solitary place. But the crowds found out about it and followed Him on foot from the towns.
When He stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had {{splanchnizomai|compassion}} on them and healed their sick.
When evening came, the disciples came to Him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is already late. Dismiss the crowds so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food.”
“They do not need to go away,” Jesus replied. “You give them something to eat.”
“We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish,” they answered.
“Bring them here to Me,” Jesus said.

And He directed the crowds to sit down on the grass. Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, He spoke a {{eulogeo|blessing}}. Then He broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people.
They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
About five thousand men were fed, besides women and children.

units.label: Walking on the water
units.note: truly You are the Son of God

verses.text: Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to the other side, while He dismissed the crowds.
After He had dismissed them, He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray. When evening came, He was there alone,
but the boat was already far from land, buffeted by the waves because the wind was against it.
During the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea.
When the disciples saw Him walking on the sea, they were terrified. “It’s a ghost!” they said, and cried out in fear.
But Jesus spoke up at once: “Take courage! {{egoeimi|It is I}}. Do not be afraid.”
“Lord, if it is You,” Peter replied, “command me to come to You on the water.”
“Come,” said Jesus. Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water, and came toward Jesus.
But when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, “Lord, save me!”
Immediately Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter. “You of little faith,” He said, “why did you doubt?”
And when they had climbed back into the boat, the wind died down.
Then those who were in the boat {{proskyneo|worshiped}} Him, saying, “Truly You are the Son of God!”

units.label: Healing at Gennesaret
units.note: all who touched Him were healed

verses.text: When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret.
And when the men of that place recognized Jesus, they sent word to all the surrounding region. People brought all the sick to Him
and begged Him just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion in one's inmost being. Though grieving John's death and seeking solitude, Jesus is moved to His core by the crowd's need, and heals and feeds them; His mercy overflows even His own sorrow.

eulogeo.gloss: To bless, give thanks, speak well of. Jesus looks to heaven and blesses the loaves before breaking and distributing them; the gestures, take, bless, break, give, echo the Passover and anticipate the Last Supper.

egoeimi.gloss: It is I, literally I am. On the sea Jesus' reassurance carries the resonance of the divine name revealed to Moses, Exodus 3:14; the One who walks the waves speaks with the voice of God, calming fear.

proskyneo.gloss: To worship, fall down before, do homage. After the storm the disciples worship Jesus and confess Him the Son of God, the response due to God alone, drawn out by His mastery over the sea.

basic.context: Hearing of John's death, Jesus withdraws to be alone, but the crowds follow, and He has compassion, healing and then feeding them. From five loaves and two fish He satisfies five thousand men plus women and children, with twelve baskets left over. That night He sends the disciples ahead, prays alone, and then comes to them walking on the storm-tossed sea. He rescues Peter, who tried and began to sink, stills the wind, and the disciples worship Him as the Son of God.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the feeding as more than a miracle of provision: the wilderness setting, the shepherd's compassion, and the take-bless-break-give pattern recall the manna, the Shepherd of Psalm 23, and point toward the Lord's Supper. Read the sea-walking as a revelation of Jesus' deity: only God treads the waves, and His words carry the divine I am. Together they answer who Jesus is.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is moved with compassion, a gut-deep mercy, even in His own grief. He blesses the loaves with the gestures that echo the Passover and the Supper to come. On the sea His words, It is I, carry the sound of the divine name, I am. And the disciples worship Him, giving Him the homage due to God, confessing Him the Son of God.
basic.typology: Jesus feeding the crowd in the wilderness fulfills the pattern of God feeding Israel with manna and pictures the Messiah's banquet. As the Shepherd of Psalm 23, He makes them lie down in green pastures. And His walking on the sea takes up what Scripture says of God alone, who treads the waves and stills the storm.
basic.christ: Jesus is the compassionate Shepherd who provides abundantly from almost nothing, the true bread who satisfies. And He is the divine Lord who walks upon the sea and speaks the name of God, mastering the chaos that terrifies His disciples. Their confession is the point: truly You are the Son of God.
basic.god: The God who fed Israel in the wilderness and who alone rules the sea is present and at work in Jesus. His compassion meets human need with overflowing abundance, and His power over creation is absolute. He is worthy of worship, and He reaches out to rescue the sinking who cry to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 16 gives the manna in the wilderness. Psalm 23 is the Shepherd who provides. Job 9 says God alone treads on the waves of the sea. And Matthew 26 echoes the take, bless, break, give of the Last Supper.
basic.oneStory: In the wake of rejection and grief, Jesus reveals His glory more brightly than ever. He is the Shepherd who feeds the hungry multitude in the wilderness and the divine Lord who walks the raging sea and rescues the sinking. The disciples fall down in worship with the confession the whole Gospel has been building toward: truly You are the Son of God, the King who provides and saves.

context.literary:
This chapter sits at the centre of Matthew's account of the Galilean ministry, and it is built from three movements that echo one another: a meal in the wilderness, a crossing of the sea, and a harvest of healings on the far shore. The first two are tied by the same pattern of dismissal. In verse 15 the disciples ask Jesus to dismiss the crowds so they can buy food; in verse 22 Jesus makes the disciples go ahead while He dismisses the crowds Himself; in verse 23 He goes up the mountain alone. The disciples' idea of what to do with the crowds is replaced by His.

The most important literary relationship is with what comes before. Chapter 14 begins with a feast at which a king, Herod, killed a prophet, 14:6 to 11. It continues with a feast at which a greater King feeds the hungry and gives life. The first meal takes place in a palace in the presence of the great, and the second in a wilderness among the poor. The first is served on a platter that holds a head, and the second on the grass with bread that is broken and shared. The reader is meant to feel the contrast.

The feeding has the same shape as Matthew's accounts of the Last Supper and the second feeding in 15:32 to 39. Four verbs run through verse 19: He took, blessed, broke and gave. The same four appear in Matthew 26:26. The twelve baskets of leftovers give the story an ending of surplus, and Jesus later refers to the count in 16:9 to 10, showing that He intended the numbers to be remembered.

The walking on the water is Matthew's own expanded version of a story told in Mark and John. Only Matthew includes Peter's walk and his rescue, and only Matthew has the whole boat worship Him and call Him Son of God. The final scene, the healing at Gennesaret, brings the movement to rest in a summary where touching the fringe of His cloak is enough. Hearing about the death of a prophet has led, over one day and night, to the full revelation of the Messiah.
context.historical:
Jesus withdrew 'privately' by boat on hearing of John's death. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee from his new city of Tiberias on the western shore of the lake, so a crossing to the eastern side, to the lands of the tetrarch Philip, may also have put distance between Jesus and the man who had just killed the Baptist. Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida, Luke 9:10, and John says the Passover was near, John 6:4, so many of those who followed on foot may have been on the road toward the festival. The 'solitary place' and 'desolate place' of verses 13 and 15 point to an uncultivated area where no market was near.

The numbers are given with a care that shows the writer wanted them tested. Five thousand 'men' were counted, which is the Greek word for males, and Matthew adds that there were also women and children, so the real number was larger. John says that the loaves were barley, John 6:9, the cheaper grain, and the fish were small fish of the sort the lake supplied. Five loaves and two fish were the meal of one family or one boy, as John tells it, and no meal for a crowd.

The sea of Galilee lies about two hundred metres below sea level and is surrounded by hills. Cold air that spills down through the valleys can raise sudden storms, and fishermen like the disciples knew this well. The Romans divided the night into four watches, and the fourth was the last, from about three to six in the morning, so Jesus came to the boat at the darkest and most exhausted hour, after hours of rowing against the wind.

The disciples' cry that it was a ghost reflects the common belief in apparitions, and the fear that follows is genuine. After they land, the people of Gennesaret, the fertile plain on the western shore, bring the sick. The 'fringe of His cloak' recalls the tassels that Jewish men were commanded to wear on the corners of their garments, Numbers 15:38 to 39. To touch the fringe was to touch the edge of the garment of a man who, as a faithful Israelite, would have worn them.
context.canonical:
The feeding looks back to two earlier meals in the wilderness. The first is the manna, when the LORD rained bread from heaven for a grumbling people, Exodus 16:4 and 16:12. The second is Elisha's miracle, in which twenty loaves fed a hundred men, with food left over 'according to the word of the LORD,' 2 Kings 4:42 to 44. Jesus' feeding surpasses both: more people, fewer loaves, and a surplus that is gathered up. The psalmist records Israel's doubt, 'Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?' Psalm 78:19, and the scene answers it. Isaiah had spoken of a banquet on the LORD's mountain for all peoples, Isaiah 25:6, and of an invitation to eat without money, Isaiah 55:1 to 2.

The picture of the shepherd stands behind the compassion of verse 14. Moses had asked for a leader so the congregation would not be like sheep without a shepherd, Numbers 27:17, and Ezekiel 34:11 to 16 promised that the LORD Himself would feed His flock and make them lie down in good pasture. Mark says that Jesus saw 'sheep without a shepherd,' Mark 6:34, and Matthew has said the same in 9:36.

The walk on the sea echoes passages that praise God for rule over the water. Job 9:8 says that God alone 'treads on the waves of the sea.' Psalm 77:19 says, 'Your path led through the sea.' Isaiah 43:2 and 43:16 promise God's presence in the waters and a path through them, and Psalm 107:23 to 30 describes sailors in a storm who cry to the LORD and are brought to harbour.

Elsewhere in the New Testament, John 6 gives the full discourse on the bread of life that follows the feeding, John 6:35, and Luke 24:30 to 35 has the risen Jesus known in the breaking of bread, using the same verbs as Matthew 14:19. Hebrews 12:2 takes up the image of keeping eyes on Jesus, though it does not mention Peter. The Lord's Supper of Matthew 26:26 is the clearest sequel.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wants his readers to ask the question that this chapter forces: who is this man? He has been rejected in his hometown and Herod has speculated about him; here the disciples themselves, for the first time as a group, answer, 'Truly You are the Son of God.' Everything in the chapter leads to that confession. The feeding shows that He is the shepherd who provides as God did in the wilderness, and the sea-walking shows that He shares the divine power over the deep. The compassion shown to the crowds and to Peter shows what kind of God this is.

He also intends to teach the disciples, and his readers, how to act. Jesus' instruction 'You give them something to eat' is a rebuke of the disciples' practical wisdom and a call to depend on Him. The bread passes through their hands to the crowd, and the church is shown as the means by which Christ feeds the world. The pause for prayer on the mountain, after a long day of healing and feeding, sets a pattern for a Lord who does not neglect fellowship with the Father in the middle of ministry.

The story of Peter is told for those who follow Jesus into the storm. It teaches that a disciple may be called out of safety by the Lord's own word, that fear of the wind can overwhelm a faith that has begun well, and that the Lord's hand is always near enough to catch. It was told to a community that would face winds of its own, and that needed to know that Jesus comes to the boat in the darkest watch.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The feeding and the walking on the sea describe unique acts of the Son of God, not standing commands to repeat them. Believers are not told to expect that bread will multiply in their hands, or to step out of a boat in a gale. What the stories prescribe is what Jesus tells His disciples in verse 16, 'You give them something to eat.' The disciples had little, five loaves and two fish, and they were asked to bring what they had to Him and to hand out what He gave. The church shares what Christ gives and does not manufacture the supply.

Peter's request, 'command me to come to You,' is carefully worded, and it is the Lord's word, 'Come,' that makes the walk possible. The scene is not an invitation to attempt dangerous things on the strength of a feeling. It is a picture of obedience to a clear command and of dependence on Him for the power to obey. It also describes a failure that is not condemned with finality. Jesus calls Peter a man of little faith and still catches him.

The narrator also describes Jesus' time alone with the Father, and this is both a description and an example of a pattern He repeated: Matthew 14:13 and 14:23 show Him seeking solitude to pray. Believers are not commanded to withdraw in every case, but the pattern shows that service flows from prayer, not the reverse. The fact that He went to the mountain after healing the sick is not a rule about rest but a window into His dependence on the Father.

debates.question: What does Jesus walking on the sea and saying It is I reveal about Him?

views.label: A disclosure of His deity
views.case: Scripture says God alone treads the waves and stills the storm; Jesus doing so, and speaking the words It is I that echo the divine name, unveils Him as God present with His people, drawing the confession Son of God.

views.label: A rescue that reveals His lordship over chaos
views.case: The scene shows Jesus as Lord over the sea, the ancient emblem of chaos and death, coming to His storm-tossed disciples to save them; His mastery over the deep marks His divine authority.

debates.bearing: Both hold that the sea-walking is a theophany, a showing of God in Jesus, so that worship and the confession of His deity are the only fitting response.

debates.question: What does Peter's walking and sinking teach?

views.label: Faith fixed on Christ, endangered by fear
views.case: Peter walks while looking to Jesus and begins to sink when he sees the wind; the lesson is that faith fastened on Christ can do the impossible, while fear and doubt make us sink.

views.label: The rescue of the sinking who cry out
views.case: The heart of the scene is that when Peter cries, Lord, save me, Jesus at once reaches out and holds him; even little faith that calls on Christ is not abandoned but caught by His hand.

debates.bearing: Both teach that we must keep our eyes on Christ amid the storm, and that when we falter and cry to Him, He is quick to save, gently rebuking our doubt while holding us fast.

debates.question: What is the feeding of the five thousand chiefly a sign of?

views.label: A new Moses and Elisha, giving bread in the wilderness
views.case: The setting, the grass, the shortage of food and the surplus all recall the manna and Elisha's loaves. The crowd in John 6:14 says, 'Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world,' which fits a prophetic reading.

views.label: The coming banquet of the messianic age
views.case: Isaiah 25:6 promises a feast for all peoples on the LORD's mountain, and Jesus' compassion for the crowd as sheep without a shepherd fulfils Ezekiel 34. The meal is a sign that the age of fulfilment has begun.

views.label: A foreshadowing of the Lord's Supper
views.case: The four verbs of verse 19 recur in Matthew 26:26, and John joins the feeding to the bread of life, John 6:35. Many interpreters from the early church onward have seen in the feeding a sign of the bread given for the life of the world.

debates.bearing: These views are not rivals. The story draws on the manna and Elisha, announces the banquet, and anticipates the Supper at once. What the text clearly says is that Jesus is the compassionate provider, and the surplus of twelve baskets shows that what He gives is more than enough.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb for compassion in verse 14 is splagchnizomai, from the word for the inner organs, the seat of deep feeling. Matthew uses it of Jesus' response to need: for the harassed crowds, 9:36, here in 14:14, for the hungry in 15:32, and for the blind men in 20:34. It is a feeling that moves to action. Here the action is healing and then feeding, so that compassion is not a mood but a mission.

The four verbs of verse 19 are in order: He took, He blessed, He broke and He gave, using lambano, eulogeo, klao and didomi. Matthew 26:26 uses the same four, so that the early church read the feeding in the light of the Supper. The verb 'blessed' is a blessing spoken over the bread, in the manner of the Jewish table prayer, so that Jesus is giving thanks to the Father for it. In the feeding of the four thousand Matthew shifts to eucharisteo, to give thanks, in 15:36, and in 26:27 uses it of the cup.

'They ate and were satisfied' translates a single verb, chortazo, which originally was used of feeding animals until they were full, and then of satisfying people. Matthew 5:6 uses its future form for those who hunger for righteousness: 'they will be filled.' The feeding is thus a living picture of a promise the Sermon had already made. And the leftovers were gathered in kophinoi, a kind of wicker basket, while in the feeding of the four thousand they are spyrides, a different word for baskets or hampers. Jesus reminds the disciples of the difference in 16:9 to 10, so the writer evidently expected the details to matter.

In verse 24 the boat is 'buffeted' by the waves, using basanizo, a verb that usually means to torment or torture. The boat is being tormented by the sea. At the heart of verse 27 stands the saying 'Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.' 'It is I' is the Greek ego eimi, literally 'I am,' which is the ordinary way to say 'It is I' and which also stands in the Greek Old Testament for the divine self-declaration, as in Isaiah 43:10 and Exodus 3:14. The words can bear both senses, and in the context of a Lord who walks on the sea and says 'Do not be afraid,' as God does in Isaiah 41:10, the second sense is hard to ignore.

Peter says 'if it is You,' then 'command me,' using keleuo, the verb for an order that a superior gives. When he begins to sink the verb is katapontizo, the word of drowning, used again in 18:6 of those cast into the depths of the sea. His cry, 'Lord, save me,' uses the verb sozo in its simplest form. Matthew's last verse of the chapter takes up the same root: all who touched His cloak were 'healed,' diasozo, a form that means to be brought safely through. Peter is saved from the sea by a hand, and the sick are brought through by a touch.

Jesus calls Peter 'You of little faith,' oligopistos, a word that Matthew uses of the disciples in 6:30, 8:26 and 16:8, and asks why he 'doubted,' from distazo, literally to stand in two minds. Matthew uses that verb only here and at the end of the Gospel, 28:17, where some of the worshippers 'doubted.' The verb for 'worshiped' in verse 33 is proskuneo, the homage given to God alone, as Jesus Himself said in Matthew 4:10.

typology.type: Bread in the wilderness, Matthew 14:15 to 21
typology.fulfillment: God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness, Exodus 16:4, and Elisha fed a hundred with twenty loaves, 2 Kings 4:42 to 44. Jesus feeds five thousand men, plus women and children, with five loaves, and gathers more than He began with. John draws out the meaning in John 6:35, 'I am the bread of life.' Paul says the rock that followed Israel was Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4, so that the wilderness feeding was already His. The correspondence is real but the escalation is steep: manna fed for a day and was gone, while He gives food that endures, John 6:27. The type is completed in the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9.

typology.type: The shepherd who makes them sit down, Matthew 14:14 to 19
typology.fulfillment: Psalm 23:2 says, 'He makes me lie down in green pastures,' and Jesus has the crowd sit on the grass. Ezekiel 34:15 promises that the LORD will 'tend My flock and make them lie down.' Moses had asked God to give Israel a shepherd, Numbers 27:17, and Matthew has already seen Jesus as the answer, 9:36. The picture is fulfilled in the Good Shepherd who gives His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and who prepares a table in the presence of enemies, Psalm 23:5. The type reaches its end in the Lamb who will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17.

typology.type: The path through the sea, Matthew 14:25
typology.fulfillment: The LORD opened a way through the Red Sea for Israel, Exodus 14:21 to 22, and the psalmist says of Him, 'Your path led through the sea... but Your footprints were not to be found,' Psalm 77:19. Isaiah 43:16 calls Him the one 'who makes a way in the sea.' Jesus does not part the water but walks across it, which places Him in the place of the God who goes before His people. The correspondence differs in that Israel crossed on dry ground while Jesus treads on the waves, and He comes not before the disciples but to them in the storm. It points to the final victory over the sea, which in Revelation 21:1 is no more.

The number of baskets matches the number of the disciples who gathered them and the number of the tribes of Israel. It is probably meant to suggest that what Jesus gives is enough for all of God's people, as the later reference in 16:9 to 10 suggests that the numbers were meant to be remembered. This is an inference and not a stated meaning, since the text does not give an interpretation. It stands at the margin of typology and should be held lightly. What is clear is the generosity: the one who feeds ends with more than He began with, and what was left over is gathered for others.

study.christ:
Jesus appears here as the compassionate Shepherd who provides. The reason for the miracle is given in a single phrase: 'He had compassion on them.' He has just heard of the death of John and sought solitude, and yet when the crowd arrives He puts His own sorrow aside and heals their sick. The Lord who is tired and grieving turns aside to those who need Him. Hebrews 4:15 says that we have a high priest who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, and this scene is an example of it.

He is the one who gives to His disciples so that they may give to others. The disciples bring what they have, five loaves and two fish, and receive it back from Him. The bread passes through their hands to the crowd, which makes them partners in His work without making them the source. That is how Christ has fed His people ever since, through His word and His table, handed on by His servants. And He is the one who is Himself the bread: John 6:35 draws the feeding into the saying 'I am the bread of life.' The Lord who breaks the loaves is also the one whose body will be broken, Matthew 26:26, and the same verbs link them.

On the lake He is the Lord of the sea. The picture of the one who 'treads on the waves,' Job 9:8, and whose path is through the sea, Psalm 77:19, is attached to Him without comment, because the Gospel assumes that the reader will recognise what is being said. His words, 'It is I,' the repeated 'Do not be afraid,' and His entry into the boat at the end of the storm all belong to the language of the LORD in the Old Testament. John says that all things were made through Him, John 1:3, and the sea that obeys is the sea He made. He does not rebuke the worship of verse 33, as Peter did when Cornelius knelt, Acts 10:25 to 26, and as the angel did in Revelation 19:10.

He is the Saviour who catches. Peter's cry, 'Lord, save me,' is the briefest prayer in the Gospel, and He answers it with an outstretched hand 'immediately.' The Lord who prayed alone on the mountain while the disciples struggled had not forgotten them, and Hebrews 7:25 says that He always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him. Luke 22:31 to 32 shows the same watchfulness for Peter at a later storm.

A caution is needed. The details of the story are not all symbols: the boat is not a code for the church in every respect, the wind is not a code for every trial, and the fourth watch is not an allegory. The passage means what it says, that Jesus is the Son of God who feeds and saves, and its ties to other texts rest on the Gospel's own language.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that He is a provider. The wilderness is the place where Israel learned that God could set a table, and Psalm 78:19 records the question they asked in unbelief. The feeding is the answer. God does not wait for the crowd to reach the village or for the supply to be adequate. He starts with what is there, a few loaves, and makes it enough. The doctrine of providence is not a vague trust that things will work out but the conviction that the Creator who made bread can multiply it, and that He cares for those who are hungry. Psalm 107:9 says, 'He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things.'

He is compassionate. The emotion Matthew names is the word for the deepest feeling, and it moves the Lord to act. That is not an accident of Jesus' personality but a revelation of the heart of God. Exodus 34:6 describes Him as compassionate and gracious, and the Son makes that visible in a crowd of sick people on a hillside. God's mercy is not a general benevolence but a response to particular need.

He is sovereign over the sea. In the Old Testament the sea is the symbol of chaos and threat, and it is God who rules it, Psalm 89:9 and Psalm 65:7. That Jesus walks on it assigns to Him what belongs to God alone. The disciples' response, worship, is the only fitting one. At the same time the story holds a tension. The Lord who rules the sea has sent His disciples into the storm, and He lets them row against the wind for hours before He comes. God's rule over the deep does not mean that His people are spared the voyage. It means that He reaches them in the fourth watch, and that He is there before the wind stops.

He is a God who tests and trains faith. 'You give them something to eat' is a test, as John 6:6 says, and 'Come' to Peter is both an invitation and a trial. He allows the failure and does not abandon the one who fails. He rebukes gently, 'why did you doubt?' and holds him. The faith that He asks for is not self-reliance but reliance on Him.

He is worthy of worship. The disciples do not simply admire the miracle. They fall down, and the Lord accepts it. For worship, the passage invites us to bring the little we have, to cry for help when we sink, and to say with the disciples what the whole Gospel has been building to: 'Truly You are the Son of God.'

crossReferences.note: The LORD promises to rain down bread from heaven to feed the grumbling Israelites in the wilderness. The feeding of the five thousand takes place in a wilderness and gives bread to a hungry people, and John 6:31 to 35 explicitly connects the miracle with the manna and with Jesus as the true bread.

Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves, with food left over according to the word of the LORD. The same pattern of a small supply, a doubtful servant and a surplus appears in Matthew, and Jesus' miracle is on a far greater scale.

The Shepherd makes His sheep lie down in green pastures, and Matthew has the crowd sit on the grass. The compassionate Jesus fills the role of the LORD who shepherds His people, providing rest and food in a place that looked desolate.

The LORD promises to search for His scattered flock and feed them in good pasture, to bind up the broken and strengthen the weak. Jesus' compassion on the crowd and His healing of the sick is the fulfilment of this promise, in which God Himself becomes the shepherd.

In the speech of Job, the creator is the one who 'alone' tramples the sea's high waves, a work no creature shares. When Jesus does it, Matthew lets the deed speak: it assigns Him a prerogative that belongs only to God, and the disciples' worship is the fitting reply.

The psalmist says that God's path led through the sea and His way through the mighty waters, though His footprints were not seen. It is a picture of the invisible leadership of God in the exodus, and Jesus' visible footsteps on the lake show the same power in a human form.

The LORD declares that His people are to believe and understand that 'I am He,' and that there is no Savior but Him. Jesus' ego eimi on the lake, together with His rescue of Peter, echoes that self-declaration and shows the Saviour who now acts in person.

At the Last Supper Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing, broke it and gave it to the disciples. The same verbs describe His action in 14:19, and the feeding of the crowd is a preview of the meal in which He gives Himself as the bread broken for many.

John tells the same two miracles and adds that the crowd wanted to make Jesus king by force, that the loaves were barley, and that the boy who had them gave them up. It deepens the account and prepares for the discourse in which Jesus says, 'I am the bread of life.'

The feeding of the four thousand follows the same pattern with seven loaves, a few fish and seven baskets left over, again from compassion. Together with 16:9 to 10 it shows that the feeding is not a one-time event but a recurring sign of Jesus' provision for Jews and Gentiles.

Sailors caught in a storm see the LORD's wonders in the deep, cry to Him in their trouble, and He calms the storm and guides them to harbour. The story of the boat and Peter's cry, 'Lord, save me,' is a living version of that psalm, with Jesus in the place of the LORD.

An earlier storm on the same lake has Jesus asleep in the boat while the disciples cry 'Lord, save us,' and the disciples wonder, 'What kind of man is this?' Chapter 14 answers the question: this is the Son of God, who now comes to the boat Himself.

study.oneStory:
From the garden of Eden to the wilderness of Sinai, the Bible shows God as the one who feeds His people. He gave Adam every tree for food, Genesis 2:16, rained bread in the desert, and promised through Isaiah a banquet on His mountain for all peoples, Isaiah 25:6. Alongside this runs the story of the sea. It is there at the beginning, dark and deep, Genesis 1:2, and it is God who divides it for Israel at the exodus, Exodus 14:21, and who rules it, Psalm 89:9. The sea becomes the picture of everything that threatens, and the question of the Old Testament is who can master it. In this chapter the two threads meet.

The feeding answers the hunger that the whole story of Israel has known, and the walking on the sea answers its fear. Both show that the God who did these things in the past is now present in a Man. The disciples' confession, 'Truly You are the Son of God,' is the first time the Twelve as a body say it, and it will be taken up by Peter at Caesarea Philippi in 16:16. The chapter is a stage in the slow dawning of recognition that fills the first half of Matthew.

It also looks ahead. The four verbs of the feeding lead to the Upper Room, and the breaking of bread is repeated in Emmaus, Luke 24:30, where the risen Lord is known by it. The crowds who eat and are satisfied prefigure the Gentiles who will feed on Him, as the feeding of the four thousand suggests. The sea that He treads is the sea over which the disciples will be sent, Matthew 28:19, and the storm that nearly takes Peter is the storm that the church will meet.

The story ends in the new creation, where there is a banquet, the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, and where there is no more sea, Revelation 21:1. The hungry will hunger no more, Revelation 7:16 to 17, and the Shepherd will lead them to springs of living water. What Jesus did on the hillside and on the lake was a sign of that final provision and that final peace, in which God Himself will wipe every tear from every eye, Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: How did Jesus respond when the disciples wanted to send the hungry crowds away?

options.text: He told the disciples to feed them, then fed thousands from five loaves and two fish.
options.note: Verses 16-21 record His command and the miraculous feeding.

options.text: He agreed and dismissed the crowds to buy food in the villages.
options.note: The opposite; He refused to send them away and fed them Himself.

options.text: He told the crowds to fast until morning.
options.note: He fed them at once rather than commanding a fast.

options.text: He sent the disciples to buy enough food for everyone.
options.note: They had only five loaves and two fish; Jesus multiplied them rather than sending the disciples to buy.

quiz.q: What was left over after the five thousand were fed?

options.text: Twelve basketfuls of broken pieces, showing the abundance of the provision.
options.note: Verse 20 records the twelve baskets left over after all were satisfied.

options.text: Just enough was used, with nothing to spare.
options.note: In fact there was abundant surplus, twelve baskets, underscoring the miracle.

options.text: A few scraps that were thrown away.
options.note: The leftovers were twelve full baskets deliberately gathered, not scraps discarded.

options.text: Nothing, because the food ran out.
options.note: All ate and were satisfied with twelve baskets left over; the food did not run out.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say as He came to the disciples on the water?

options.text: Take courage, It is I, do not be afraid, words carrying the resonance of the divine name.
options.note: Verse 27 gives His reassurance, echoing the I am of God's self-revelation.

options.text: Nothing; He simply climbed into the boat.
options.note: He spoke first to calm their terror before anything else.

options.text: A rebuke for their being out on the water at night.
options.note: He reassured them rather than rebuking them for the crossing He had commanded.

options.text: A command to row harder against the wind.
options.note: He calmed their fear and later stilled the wind; He did not tell them to row harder.

quiz.q: What happened when Peter walked toward Jesus on the water?

options.text: He walked while looking to Jesus, began to sink in fear, cried out, and was caught by Jesus' hand.
options.note: Verses 29-31 show his faith, his fear, and his rescue.

options.text: He walked the whole way without any difficulty.
options.note: He did walk, but began to sink when afraid; the rescue is central.

options.text: He refused to leave the boat at all.
options.note: He did step out and walk before beginning to sink.

options.text: He sank and drowned in the sea.
options.note: Jesus immediately reached out and took hold of him; he did not drown.

quiz.q: How did the disciples respond after Jesus stilled the wind?

options.text: They worshiped Him, saying, Truly You are the Son of God.
options.note: Verse 33 records their worship and confession.

options.text: They were relieved but said nothing about who He was.
options.note: They did more than feel relief; they worshiped and confessed Him the Son of God.

options.text: They argued about how He had done it.
options.note: Their response was worship and confession, not debate.

options.text: They asked Him to leave them as the Gadarenes had.
options.note: They worshiped Him rather than asking Him to depart.

questions: Jesus felt compassion for the crowds even in His own grief over John. How does His mercy in the midst of sorrow encourage you to bring your needs to Him?
The disciples saw only five loaves and two fish, but Jesus saw enough to feed thousands. Where do you see only your lack, and how might you offer what little you have to Him?
On the sea Jesus said, It is I, do not be afraid. What storm are you facing where you need to hear His voice and fix your eyes on Him?
Peter began to sink when he looked at the wind instead of Jesus, yet was caught the moment he cried out. When you falter, do you cry to Christ to save you, trusting He will hold you fast?
The disciples worshiped Jesus as the Son of God after seeing His power. How does a fresh sight of who Jesus is move you to worship Him this week?

translationNotes.note: The fourth watch of the night was between three and six in the morning, the darkest, most exhausting hours, when Jesus came to the struggling disciples.
It is I renders the Greek ego eimi, I am, which carries the resonance of the divine name revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14.
Truly You are the Son of God is a high confession of worship, anticipating Peter's fuller confession in Matthew 16:16.
